remarks: Boilers are regulated by a separate Boilers Department, independent of the Factories Department.
No labour court involvement in factory licensing; only Occupational Safety and Health provisions under the Factories Act apply.

Factories, Pollution Control and Labour departments each conduct separate inspections/certifications for the same establishment; the expert views integrating these into a single joint inspection or license as not feasible since each department evaluates a distinct technical aspect.

findings.text: Factory license applications must be disposed of within a statutory 7 working day timeline, uniformly applied across hazardous, non-hazardous and general category industries.

Site inspection by the Inspector of Factories remains an offline, physical process; virtual/digital inspection is not currently used because physical inspection is considered a more value-added exercise.

The Stability Certificate requirement is frequently a point of deficiency — some applicants assume it is not required for new buildings and do not submit it, leading to a deficiency/query (NCS) on the application.

The expert suggested improving applicant awareness and guidance on mandatory documents, including the Stability Certificate, at the application stage to reduce deficiency queries and processing delays.

All inspection observations and field-visit findings are uploaded to the public domain through the Central Inspection System portal, giving complete transparency and making reports accessible to the public.

Factories employing more than 20 workers require a license; those with fewer than 20 are generally exempt, except specified hazardous categories notified under Section 85(1) (e.g. rice mills, dal mills, saw mills/timber-cutting units, small engineering works) which require a license even with fewer than 10 workers.
Selection for random inspection follows a risk/capital-based allocation under the Central Inspection System (CIS).

Factories, Pollution Control and Labour departments each conduct separate inspections/certifications for the same establishment; the expert considers integrating these into a single joint inspection infeasible since each evaluates a distinct technical aspect.
License fee is charged per a slab-based schedule linked to installed horsepower and number of workers employed, paid online.

Renewal requires annual online fee payment before 31 December; no fresh physical inspection is required unless there is an amendment to activity (e.g. additional manufacturing line, increase in horsepower), which requires a Revision License (RVL) with revised plan approval.
The expert recommended exploring the feasibility of digital/virtual inspection for low-risk renewal cases, while retaining physical inspection for high-risk or first-time cases.

The expert recommended improving applicant guidance on which documents carry forward from the plan-approval stage (CAF-1) versus what must be freshly submitted for the license (CAF-2), to reduce document deficiencies.
If an application is not disposed of within the 7 working day statutory timeline, the concerned Inspector is required to submit an explanation to the Commissioner of Industries.

About 50-60% of the information in the factory building plan (CAF-1) is auto-populated into the license application (CAF-2), reducing duplicate data entry, though the remainder must still be submitted afresh.

Compliance with siting norms (factory should not be near water bodies, schools, colleges or residential areas) and stack-emission norms (monitored by the Pollution Control Board and cross-checked during inspection) is checked at the plan-approval stage.

gaps.text: No exact fee figures or slab thresholds (horsepower/worker ranges and corresponding fee amounts) are given for the factory license fee.
The correction period for minor deviations is given inconsistently as 'a stipulated period (e.g., 15 days/1 week)' without one definitive figure.
Complete public disclosure of all inspection observations and field-visit findings via the Central Inspection System portal.

Expert recommended improving applicant guidance on mandatory documents (e.g. Stability Certificate) and on which CAF-1 items carry forward versus need fresh submission in CAF-2, to reduce deficiency queries.

The document does not explicitly state whether the applicant must visit any government office in person; it only states application/fee submission is online and that the Inspector conducts a physical site visit.
The frequency/rate of deficiency queries (NCS) relating to the Stability Certificate is described only as 'frequently' with no actual figure.

remarks: Discussion conducted virtually on 6 August 2026 (approx. 15 minutes).
The Andhra Pradesh Factories (draft) Rules came into force on the same date as this discussion (6 August 2026).
CTE (Consent to Establish, from the Pollution Control Board) and Factory Plan Approval are processed in parallel, not sequentially — a point specifically clarified by the expert.
Immediately following this session, the discussion continued on to cover the Factory License service.

findings.text: The Department of Factories is required to grant Factory Plan Approval within a statutory 7 working day timeline from receipt of the application.
Application filing, document upload and approval are all carried out fully online through the Single Desk Portal; no offline steps were reported by the expert for this service.

The Factory Plan Approval application is filed in parallel with the Consent to Establish (CTE) application to the Pollution Control Board, not as a sequential, later step — a point the expert specifically clarified.

A nominal processing fee applies, tiered by slab from roughly ₹100 for lower-capacity plants to ₹1,000 for higher-capacity plants, with the approving authority also tiered by the fee/connected-load slab.
The expert noted that audio quality during the discussion made the exact fee slab boundaries difficult to confirm, and recommended verifying the figures against the AP Factories Rules.

No colour-coded (white/green/orange/red) risk classification applies to Factory Plan Approval; instead, machinery load determines scrutiny level — plants using machinery above 30 HP require Department of Factories approval, while those below 30 HP do not.
The expert did not identify any redundant or duplicate requirements; the documentation sought (site plan, detailed plan, index of machinery) was described as the essential minimum needed.

The expert views existing technical requirements (spacing/setback norms, fire-safety provisions, ventilation/window norms per the National Building Code) as basic minimum safety requirements rather than a burden, cautioning that removing them could increase the accident rate.
The Department is in the process of empanelling architects, planners and developers, which is expected to reduce the time the Department spends on plan scrutiny once operational.
The expert recommended expediting and operationalising the empanelment system for architects, planners and developers to reduce departmental time spent on plan scrutiny.
The expert recommended clearly publishing the fee slabs and corresponding approving authority (DCIF / JCIF / CIF) to improve transparency for applicants.
The expert recommended continuing to align technical scrutiny norms with the National Building Code, the OSH Code 2020, and the newly notified AP Factories Rules.
The ongoing empanelment of architects, planners and developers in Andhra Pradesh was highlighted by the expert as a forthcoming improvement that could be considered by other states.
The Andhra Pradesh Factories (draft) Rules came into force on the same date as this discussion (6 August 2026).

Validity period for the Factory Plan Approval was not discussed by the expert.
The deemed approval provision was not discussed by the expert for this service.
Post-approval compliance checklist was not covered in this discussion; the session moved directly to the Factory License service.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board (APPCB), Government of Andhra Pradesh — regional office

portal.name: Single Desk/Single Window portal, linked to the APPCB website

timeline.basis: Service Level Agreement (SLA) timelines by CPCB risk category: Red 21 days, Orange 14 days, Green 7 days; auto-renewal for eligible White/Green units via self-declaration is faster, around 3 days of scrutiny
timeline.text: Renewed Consent to Operate is issued within applicable SLA timelines that vary by risk category — 21 days for Red, 14 days for Orange and 7 days for Green category units — with auto-renewal for eligible White/Green units completing in roughly 3 days.

documents: Details of raw materials, products and effluent/emission generation
Hazardous waste generation and disposal mode details
Condition-wise compliance report against the previous consent
Self-declaration confirming continued compliance with existing consent conditions (for White/Green auto-renewal)
licenses.documentsNote: Where there is no change in process, products or production since the earlier consent cycle, previously submitted data/documents are auto-fetched on the portal for the renewal application, reducing the burden of resubmission.

deemedApproval.text: There is no formal 'deemed approval' clause as such, but APPCB has operationalised an equivalent through auto-renewal of CTO for White and Green category units: on submission of a self-certificate declaring compliance with all existing consent conditions, renewal is granted without a fresh inspection.

validity.text: Validity varies by risk category. Green category units are granted Consent to Operate valid for 15 years, with no mandatory auto-renewal requirement within that period (renewal thereafter is based on the unit's own self-application). Red/Orange category units renew on a shorter cyclical basis linked to their existing consent period, with auto-renewal available for White/Green category units before expiry via self-declaration.

fees.text: Fee is based on the project cost/category (and, for mining activity, on the extent of mining/production) as stipulated by government/CPCB norms, paid online through the single window portal. There is no separate inspection fee; the fee covers processing of the application only.

steps.title: Apply online through Single Desk/Single Window portal
steps.note: Minimum required data entered flows through to the APPCB portal (ap.mms.nic.in).

steps.title: Upload required documents/data
steps.note: Raw material and product details, effluent/emission particulars, hazardous waste generation, treatment/disposal mode, and compliance report against earlier consent conditions.

steps.title: APPCB scrutinises the application
steps.note: Red/Orange category units are inspected; White/Green category units eligible for auto-renewal require only a self-declaration, with no inspection.

steps.title: Inspection for Red/Orange category units
steps.note: Board officials inspect the unit and verify compliance/pollution-control system status.

steps.title: Renewed Consent to Operate issued
steps.note: Within the applicable SLA timeline (Red 21 days; Orange 14 days; Green 7 days).

ed.location: APPCB Regional Office (Jurisdiction: Eluru and Krishna districts)

remarks: The Consent to Operate renewal process is independent of the Factory License; the two are separate applications with no interlinkage, APPCB processes only the pollution-control consent.
Where groundwater is used, the industry additionally needs to obtain separate permission for its extraction/use.
There is no separate inspection fee; the statutory fee covers processing of the application only, not inspection.

findings.text: APPCB strictly follows SLA timelines by risk category: Red 21 days, Orange 14 days, Green 7 days, with auto-renewal for White/Green units completing faster, around 3 days of scrutiny.
The expert noted an applicant satisfaction level of around 85% against the SLA timelines.

The renewal application, supporting documents and fee payment are submitted only through the Single Desk/Single Window portal; manual/offline submission of consent renewal applications is not accepted.

Where there is no change in process or products since the previous consent cycle, APPCB auto-fetches the same previously submitted data for the renewal application instead of requiring fresh resubmission, which the expert noted reduces duplication.
Red/Orange category units are physically inspected by board officials to verify compliance; White/Green category units eligible for auto-renewal require only a self-declaration, with no inspection.

Units are classified Red/Orange/Green/White based on CPCB's industrial-sector classification, driven purely by the nature/activity of the industry (pollution potential) rather than geographical location; this classification determines the SLA timeline and whether inspection is required.

Applications get stuck or delayed where the applicant does not pay the requisite fee or does not upload the full set of required documents on the portal; APPCB then raises a clarification and processing halts until the deficiency is corrected.
APPCB has set up a help desk at the regional office to assist entrepreneurs with documentation and the application process, which the expert felt has eased this difficulty considerably.

Real-time/online continuous emission and effluent monitoring systems (OCEMS) for major industries are integrated with APPCB's central server, with automatic deviation alerts, enabling close oversight without relying solely on periodic inspection.

Major industries are required to maintain a real-time online effluent/emission monitoring system (OCEMS) connected to APPCB's central server, along with periodic calibration of the monitoring equipment, and must submit a compliance report every 6 months with a NABL-accredited laboratory analysis report.

The expert recommended continuing and considering extending the auto-renewal (self-certification, no-inspection) model currently available to White/Green category units to more categories where risk profile permits, to further reduce processing time and administrative burden.
Active promotion of circular economy and zero-waste/zero-discharge approaches by government was cited by the expert as a positive direction for industry.
The Consent to Operate renewal process is independent of the Factory License; the two are separate applications with no interlinkage, as APPCB processes only the pollution-control consent.
Where groundwater is used, the industry additionally needs to obtain separate permission for its extraction/use, beyond the Consent to Operate.

Fee is based on project cost/category (and, for mining activity, on extent of mining/production) per government/CPCB norms; there is no separate inspection fee, the fee covers processing of the application only.

The '85% applicant satisfaction' figure against SLA timelines is given without a stated source, survey methodology, or time period.
Dedicated help desk at the APPCB regional office to assist applicants with documentation and the application process.
Real-time online continuous emission/effluent monitoring (OCEMS) integrated with APPCB's central server, with automatic deviation alerts and periodic equipment calibration.
Expert recommended extending the auto-renewal (self-certification, no-inspection) model currently limited to White/Green category units to more categories where the risk profile permits.
